title: Student Loans 2026: Federal vs Private Loans Explained
description: Learn about student loans in 2026. Compare federal and private loans to make the best choice for your education.
body:
What is the difference between federal and private student loans?

Federal student loans are funded by the government and offer fixed interest rates, income-driven repayment plans, and forgiveness options. Private student loans are offered by banks and credit unions, with rates based on your credit. Federal loans generally offer more protections.

Which should I choose?

Maximize federal loans first, as they offer more flexible repayment and forgiveness options. Use private loans only if you need additional funding after exhausting federal options. Compare rates and terms carefully.

How do I apply for federal loans?

Complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) to determine your eligibility for federal loans, grants, and work-study. Your school will use the FAFSA to create a financial aid package.

title: Student Loan Repayment Plans 2026: Which Is Right for You?
description: Learn about student loan repayment plans in 2026. Compare standard, income-driven, and extended plans.
body:
What repayment plans are available?

Federal student loans offer several repayment plans: Standard (fixed payments over 10 years), Graduated (payments start low and increase), Extended (up to 25 years), and Income-Driven Repayment (IDR) plans that base payments on your income.

What is income-driven repayment?

Income-driven repayment plans cap your monthly payment at a percentage of your discretionary income. After 20-25 years of qualifying payments, any remaining balance is forgiven. These plans are helpful if you have high debt relative to income.

How do I choose a plan?

Consider your income, debt amount, and financial goals. Use the loan simulator on StudentAid.gov to compare plans. You can change plans at any time, so choose one that fits your current situation.

title: Student Loan Forgiveness 2026: Programs You Should Know
description: Learn about student loan forgiveness programs in 2026. Understand PSLF, income-driven forgiveness, and other options.
body:
What student loan forgiveness programs are available?

Key programs include Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) for public service workers, income-driven repayment forgiveness after 20-25 years, and Teacher Loan Forgiveness for educators. Each has specific eligibility requirements.

What is Public Service Loan Forgiveness?

PSLF forgives the remaining balance on federal Direct Loans after 120 qualifying monthly payments while working full-time for a qualifying public service employer. This includes government and nonprofit organizations.

How do I qualify for forgiveness?

Ensure you have eligible federal loans, are on a qualifying repayment plan, and work for a qualifying employer. Submit the PSLF form annually and track your qualifying payments. Review program requirements carefully.

title: Refinancing Student Loans 2026: Is It Right for You?
description: Learn about refinancing student loans in 2026. Compare benefits, risks, and when refinancing makes sense.
body:
What is student loan refinancing?

Refinancing combines your student loans into a new loan with a private lender, often at a lower interest rate. This can lower your monthly payment or help you pay off debt faster. However, refinancing federal loans means losing federal protections.

When does refinancing make sense?

Refinancing makes sense if you have a strong credit score, stable income, and can get a significantly lower rate. It is less beneficial if you rely on federal benefits like income-driven repayment or forgiveness.

What are the risks?

Refinancing federal loans into private loans means losing access to federal repayment plans, forgiveness programs, and deferment options. Consider these trade-offs carefully before refinancing.

title: Financial Aid and Scholarships 2026: How to Get Free Money for College
description: Learn about financial aid and scholarships in 2026. How to find and apply for free money for college.
body:
What types of financial aid are available?

Financial aid includes grants, scholarships, work-study, and loans. Grants and scholarships are free money that does not need to be repaid. Work-study provides part-time jobs. Loans must be repaid with interest.

How do I find scholarships?

Search scholarship databases, check with your school's financial aid office, and look for local and niche scholarships. Apply early and often. Many scholarships have specific eligibility criteria, so tailor your applications.

How do I apply for financial aid?

Complete the FAFSA to apply for federal aid. Many states and schools also use the FAFSA for their aid programs. Some private scholarships require separate applications. Submit all required materials by the deadlines.
